mission.s1.title: Brute force investigation
mission.s1.brief: The SIEM flagged unusual SSH activity on the web server srv-web-01 at 03:14. You have a shell on the server. Find who attacked it, find out whether they got in, and contain the incident. Start by reading the shift lead's note: `cat notes.txt`
mission.s1.obj.ip: Identify the attacking IP address (submit ip …)
mission.s1.obj.block: Block the attacker on the host firewall (ufw)
mission.s1.hint.1: Failed SSH logins are written to `/var/log/auth.log` with the phrase “Failed password”. Try: `grep "Failed password" /var/log/auth.log | head`
mission.s1.hint.2: Count failures per IP: `grep "Failed password" /var/log/auth.log | grep -oE "[0-9]+\.[0-9]+\.[0-9]+\.[0-9]+" | sort | uniq -c | sort -nr`
mission.s1.hint.3: Look for a successful login from the same IP: `grep Accepted /var/log/auth.log`. Firewall and account changes need sudo: `sudo ufw deny from <ip>`, `sudo usermod -L <user>`.
mission.s1.debrief.1: A brute-force attack shows up in auth.log as many “Failed password” lines from one source in a short time. Counting failures per IP (`grep | sort | uniq -c | sort -nr`) separates a real attack (142 attempts) from background noise (the 4-attempt scan and admins mistyping passwords).
mission.s1.debrief.2: The attacker eventually logged in as “backup”, a system account that had a password and a login shell. Attackers target accounts like this because nobody watches them.
mission.s1.debrief.3: Blocking the IP stops new attempts, but the account was already compromised, so you also had to lock it. Containment covers both the source and the foothold.
mission.s1.debrief.4: In production you would prevent this with key-only SSH (`PasswordAuthentication no`), fail2ban or rate limiting, MFA, and no login shell for service accounts — then investigate what “backup” did after 03:19.
fb.s1.notIp: That is not a valid IPv4 address.
fb.s1.ipCorrect: Correct — that IP is behind the attack.
fb.s1.decoy: Only 4 attempts from that IP before it gave up. That is internet background noise, not the attack.
fb.s1.internal: That address is in our internal 10.0.0.0/8 range — it is one of us.
fb.s1.ipWrong: That IP is not behind the attack. Count failed logins per IP.
fb.s1.userCorrect: Correct — the attacker logged in as “backup”.
fb.s1.root: root was targeted, but every attempt on it failed. Look for an “Accepted” login.
fb.s1.legit: That user logged in normally from the internal network.
fb.s1.userWrong: That account was not broken into. Look for a successful login from the attacker's IP.
fb.s1.blockedInternal: Warning: you just blocked an internal address. That could cut off a colleague.
fb.s1.blockedOther: Rule added, but that is not the attacking IP.
fb.s1.lockedWrong: That account was not compromised. Locking it could break a legitimate service or user.

mission.n1.title: Harden the access switch
mission.n1.brief: A visitor plugged a laptop into a free wall jack in the meeting room and got onto the office network. You are on the console of SW-ACCESS-01. Shut down every unused port, lock the reception port to the reception PC with port security, and save the configuration so it survives a reboot. Ports Fa0/1–Fa0/4 and Gi0/1 are in use; Fa0/5–Fa0/12 are unused wall jacks.
mission.n1.obj.unused: Shut down all unused ports (Fa0/5–Fa0/12) without cutting off devices in use
mission.n1.obj.portsec: Fa0/1: access mode + port security (max 1 MAC, sticky, violation shutdown)
mission.n1.obj.save: Save the running configuration to startup-config
mission.n1.hint.1: Start with `enable` then `show interfaces status` to see which ports are connected. To configure many ports at once: `configure terminal` then `interface range fa0/5 - 12` then `shutdown`.
mission.n1.hint.2: Port security only works on access ports. On `interface fa0/1`: `switchport mode access`, `switchport port-security`, `switchport port-security maximum 1`, `switchport port-security mac-address sticky`, `switchport port-security violation shutdown`.
mission.n1.hint.3: Changes live only in RAM until you save them. Leave config mode with `end`, then `copy running-config startup-config` (or `write memory`). Check your work with `show running-config` and `show port-security`.
mission.n1.debrief.1: Every unused port is a free network connection for anyone who walks by. Shutting them down (and enabling them only when needed) is one of the cheapest controls you can apply.
mission.n1.debrief.2: Port security with a sticky MAC learns the reception PC's address and shuts the port if any other device is plugged in. It stops casual plug-ins, but MAC addresses can be spoofed, so real networks add 802.1X authentication.
mission.n1.debrief.3: IOS refuses port security on a dynamic port because a port negotiating a trunk could carry many VLANs. Setting `switchport mode access` first is also a hardening step: it stops VLAN-hopping through DTP.
mission.n1.debrief.4: The running-config is lost on reboot unless you copy it to startup-config. Unsaved hardening is one of the most common findings in network audits.
fb.n1.cutOff: You shut down a port that a device is using. Bring it back with `no shutdown`.
fb.n1.maxHigh: Maximum above 1 lets extra devices share the reception port.
mission.c1.title: Fix the SQL injection
mission.c1.brief: A penetration test logged in as admin on the staff portal using the username `admin' --` and no password. The login function builds its SQL query by gluing user input into the string. Rewrite it so the database receives the values separately from the query, then run the security tests. Normal logins must keep working.
mission.c1.obj.works: Normal login (correct and wrong password) still works
mission.c1.hint.1: The problem is the + username + inside the SQL string. Whatever the user types becomes part of the SQL command itself.
mission.c1.hint.2: Use placeholders in the query text: `WHERE username = ? AND password_hash = ?` and pass the values as the second argument of db.query.
mission.c1.hint.3: The fixed call looks like: `db.query(sql, [username, hash(password)])`. Keep the order of the values the same as the order of the placeholders.
mission.c1.debrief.1: With concatenation, the payload admin' -- closes the string and comments out the password check, so the query becomes “find user admin”. The database cannot tell your SQL apart from the attacker's.
mission.c1.debrief.2: Parameterized queries send the SQL and the values separately. The database compiles the query first and treats every value only as data, so quotes and comments in a username are harmless.
mission.c1.debrief.3: Filtering or escaping quotes yourself is fragile: encodings, other quote characters and second-order injection get past it. Placeholders are the fix; input validation is an extra layer, not a replacement.
mission.c1.debrief.4: The same rule applies in every language and driver: PreparedStatement in Java, cursor.execute(sql, params) in Python, PDO prepared statements in PHP, and ORMs that bind values for you.
fb.c1.still: The tests still bypass the login. User input is still part of the SQL text.
fb.c1.filter: Filtering characters does not fix SQL injection. Use placeholders and pass the values separately.
fb.c1.broken: Injection is blocked, but normal login no longer works. Check the placeholders and the values array.
mission.k1.title: Exposed storage bucket
mission.k1.brief: A security researcher reported that one of the company's storage buckets is readable by anyone on the internet and contains employee data. You have the NexusCloud CLI on the bastion host. Find the bucket, make it private, and turn on encryption — without taking down the public website, which is also served from storage.
mission.k1.hint.1: List buckets with `nxcloud storage ls`, then look inside each one with `nxcloud storage ls <bucket>`. Check who can read it with `nxcloud storage get-bucket-policy <bucket>`.
mission.k1.hint.2: Two buckets are public. Only one of them should be: the website. Which one holds payroll and bank data?
mission.k1.hint.3: Lock it down with `nxcloud storage put-public-access-block <bucket> --block-all`, then `nxcloud storage put-encryption <bucket> --algorithm AES256`.
mission.k1.debrief.1: A policy with Principal "*" means anyone on the internet. Misconfigured storage like this is behind many of the largest real-world data leaks — no hacking needed, just a URL.
mission.k1.debrief.2: A public access block is a guardrail on top of the policy: even if someone later adds a public policy by mistake, the block keeps the bucket private.
mission.k1.debrief.3: Not every public bucket is a problem — the website is meant to be public. Security work means understanding the purpose of each resource before changing it, so you don't cause an outage while fixing a leak.
mission.k1.debrief.4: Encryption at rest protects against stolen disks and some provider-side access, but it would not have stopped this leak: the data was served decrypted to anyone allowed to read it. Access control comes first.
fb.k1.found: Correct — that bucket holds payroll and bank data and is public.
fb.k1.websiteIntended: That bucket is public on purpose: it serves the company website.
fb.k1.notPublic: That bucket is not publicly readable.
fb.k1.noSuch: There is no bucket with that name.
fb.k1.websiteDown: Warning: you just made the website bucket private. The public website is now down.
mission.f1.title: Evidence integrity
mission.f1.brief: In a procurement fraud case, the defense claims the digital evidence was altered after it was seized. The hashes of every file were recorded at seizure. Verify the evidence folder, find the file that changed, and use its metadata to find which account modified it.
mission.f1.obj.file: Find the file that no longer matches its recorded hash
mission.f1.obj.user: Find the account that last modified it
mission.f1.hint.1: Read `cat custody.txt`, then look at the recorded hashes with `cat SHA256SUMS`. Compute a file's hash with `sha256sum <file>`.
mission.f1.hint.2: Check every file at once: `sha256sum -c SHA256SUMS`.
mission.f1.hint.3: Metadata shows who edited a document: `exiftool <file>`. Look for “Last Modified By” and compare the Modify Date with the seizure time.
mission.f1.debrief.1: A cryptographic hash is a fingerprint: changing one character produces a completely different SHA-256. Recording hashes at seizure is how investigators prove evidence was not changed afterwards.
mission.f1.debrief.2: The invoice amount was raised from 48,500 to 148,500 and the bank account was changed — the hash mismatch proves the file is not the one that was seized.
mission.f1.debrief.3: The metadata shows the edit happened at 23:47 on 31 October, after seizure, by m.farouk. Metadata is useful but can be forged, so investigators corroborate it with logs and other sources.
mission.f1.debrief.4: Chain of custody — who held the evidence, when, and how it was protected — is what makes digital evidence admissible. Write blockers, hashing and sealed storage all serve that goal.
fb.f1.fileOk: Correct — that file's hash does not match.
fb.f1.fileWrong: That file still matches its recorded hash.
fb.f1.userOk: Correct — that account modified the file after seizure.
fb.f1.author: That account created the document. Look for who modified it last.
fb.f1.userWrong: That is not the account in the file's metadata.
mission.x1.title: Decode the intercept
mission.x1.brief: A message was intercepted from a compromised mail server. The suspects believe it is encrypted, but it is only encoded in several layers. Peel the layers off one by one with terminal tools to recover the proof string and the meeting time.
mission.x1.obj.flag: Recover the proof string (submit flag NEXUS{…})
mission.x1.obj.time: Find the meeting time (submit time HH:MM)
mission.x1.hint.1: Look at the file: `cat intercept.txt`. Only the characters 0–9 and a–f? That is hex. Turn hex back into bytes with `xxd -r -p`.
mission.x1.hint.2: The result ends with = and uses A–Z, a–z, 0–9, + and /: that is Base64. Chain it: `cat intercept.txt | xxd -r -p | base64 -d`.
mission.x1.hint.3: The text now looks like letters shifted by 13 places (ARKHF instead of NEXUS): that is ROT13. Add `| tr 'A-Za-z' 'N-ZA-Mn-za-m'`.
mission.x1.debrief.1: Hex, Base64 and ROT13 are encodings, not encryption: there is no key. Anyone who recognizes the format can reverse it, which is why stacking them adds almost no security.
mission.x1.debrief.2: Recognizing formats is a core skill: hex uses only 0–9 and a–f, Base64 uses A–Z a–z 0–9 + / and often ends with =, and ROT13 keeps word shapes but scrambles letters.
mission.x1.debrief.3: Real encryption (AES, ChaCha20) uses a secret key; without it, the output looks random and cannot be peeled off with tools like these.
mission.x1.debrief.4: Attackers and malware use layered encoding to slip past simple filters. Analysts decode it step by step exactly like this, often with tools such as CyberChef.
fb.x1.flagWrong: That is not the proof string.
fb.x1.stillRot: Close — that is still ROT13. Shift the letters back by 13.
fb.x1.timeWrong: That is not the meeting time in the message.
